title: One Screen Evenings. The Experiment That Slowed the House Down
body: The house rule is one sentence. In the evening, from dinner to bed, one screen at a time in the living room. Not no screens. One. The television or the laptop or the phone, never two, never three. It started as an experiment three months ago and it has survived contact with reality, which is more than I can say for most rules this house has passed. The problem it solved had a shape I only saw on a Tuesday. Four people in one room. The television on for the football. My laptop open for a thing I was definitely about to finish. One phone showing a video with the sound on, no headphones, because the person holding it was following two streams at once. And the specific silence of a family that is together and absent, four bodies, one room, six screens of attention scattered across the building like tenants. The rule is not nostalgia and it is not virtue. It is bandwidth. Attention, it turns out, is a room too, and one screen at a time is just civilized occupancy limits. The first evenings under the rule were almost funny. When the television had the room, the laptop went to the desk, and the desk is cold in winter, so the laptop lost. When someone needed the laptop, the television asked the room if anyone objected, and the room negotiated, and negotiation, which had rusted shut sometime around the second screen entering our lives, started to move again. That is the unexpected result. The rule did not primarily reduce screen time. It forced choice, and choice forced conversation, and conversation turned out to be the thing all those parallel screens had been quietly replacing. We now argue about what to watch. This sounds like a bug. It is the feature. People who want different things have to say so, in words, out loud, to other people, and then someone compromises, and the compromise is a tiny act of family architecture that no streaming algorithm will ever perform for you. The phones were the hardest. A phone is not a screen, the phone argues. The phone is a phone. The phone is a clock, a camera, a flashlight, a dictionary, and the argument is technically true and practically false. The working compromise is the shelf. There is a shelf by the door where phones live in the evening, available, public, walkable, like a coat rack. Need the dictionary. Walk to the coat rack, take the coat, come back. The friction is small and the friction is the point. Failures to report honestly. Guests find the rule strange and we suspend it, which is correct, hospitality outranks policy. One teenager in this house has negotiated a headphones exception for music, which is not a screen, and the negotiation was so well argued that the exception is now permanent, and this too is the feature. And on the worst Thursday of the month, when everyone is exhausted, the rule collapses for one evening, everyone returns to their corners, and by Friday the corners feel lonely enough that the rule returns without enforcement. The house is slower now. Slower is the honest word. The evenings have a floor under them instead of a trapdoor. And once or twice a week, all four of us are in front of the same screen, laughing at the same thing at the same second, which is either the most old-fashioned thing in the world or the most radical. I no longer care which. The room is occupied by its residents again.
